utterances.text: All right. Now, while we're at this, this is what's in the rules. Tell us what you had available, that is, concretely, what did this particular battalion have available at the time. Or you may want to go with what you did not have. That may be quicker.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have most of this. I can show you what I did have. First of all, I wish to emphasise that the battalion was defending an area much broader than 5 kilometres; it was closer to 10 kilometres. So my battalion was defending two areas like this. Of all these enumerated units, I only --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down, please. Please slow down, because it has to be translated and we don't want to miss a word. Okay. So first of all -- let me walk you through this. It might be easier. With respect to the length, it says here "3 to 5 kilometres." What was the length of territory that you were required to cover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So, twice the amount than what the rules require?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, on the bottom half of that page we talked about the second echelon. This would be the second echelon defence line. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Second echelon company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you have any of it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a command post and next to the command post I had my logistical platoon. And I had mortars. But all that means little without this second echelon company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going to the top part, tell us slowly one by one what you did not have.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have combat support. I have this line, only the first line of defence. All this behind within the framework of companies I did not have. I didn't have mortars, nor did I have any anti-armour weapons within companies, nor did I have the second-echelon company or the light artillery rocket platoon. So many of the things from this general scheme were lacking in my structure in those days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now -- now that we've covered this, going back to the rules, incidentally before we leave this diagram, we see that the length is 3 to 5. The width or the depth, that would be going backwards or --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 3 kilometres, 2 to 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But if we went -- if you look at the last paragraph of paragraph number 321, what about if the area is mountainous, the terrain?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for mountainous terrain, it was emphasised that the area of defence for a battalion could be even over 5 kilometres, considering the defence is usually organised across separate company areas, with each company closing off separate directions, which means that only under these circumstances, if the general disposition is met, only under those circumstances can a battalion defend an area broader than 5 kilometres on mountainous terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Were you able, sir? Concretely, were you able to exceed the 5 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what other paragraphs do you want to draw our attentions to? Let me just speed up a little bit. I notice that from --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've noticed this -- the role of the second-echelon company, para 328.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And para 327 would have what the first-echelon company would require and 328 talks about the second echelon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So basically what you've already discussed earlier with the diagram we can find in these paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, did you have a depth at the time? In light of the terrain that you had to cover, which was twice the amount you told us, 10 kilometres versus 3 to 5, with the men that you had available, with no second echelon, did you have a particular depth that you had to cover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have a specific depth. I wasn't able to cover it anyway, so I didn't have any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So then it won't be necessary to go to the map for you to draw out the depth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I believe that will be it for the -- for these notes. Now, if we could go into -- no, we'll stick with -- if I can hand you the next document, which is P391. If you could take a look at that. Now, just look at it very quickly. Do you recognise the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an analysis of combat readiness for the first half of 1995. It's dated 4 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Have you had a chance to look at this document before coming here today to testify, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from seeing it at the proofing session with you, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. But you have seen it -- you saw it at the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could look at this. And if you could draw our attention to contents in this particular analysis of combat readiness that you found relevant to the discussions here today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I would single out here to corroborate that previous accession that we had to stretch ourselves thin beyond the extent of our possibilities is found here on page 2. It is emphasised that the great breadth, in brackets, around 43 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this is -- our pages are different. So this would be ERN for the English 00716536. All right. So what do you want to draw our attention to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to draw your attention to the point which emphasises that the brigade was defending an area 43 kilometres long. By any standard, by any rule, such a wide area is impossible to defend successfully. To defend an area of that width, three brigades would be needed. And then on page --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to stick -- step by step. Here we say -- here it says: "Great width (about 43 kilometres) of the area of responsibility." So here we have a term which you have told us doesn't exist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a term which -- first of all, it is not a professional term. But during that period it was used. I cannot say it wasn't, and you can see from the document, it was used occasionally. But it was used probably because some people found it easy to use this acronym. It is in essence an inadequate term.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the rules for a brigade, the brigade rules?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we were to go into those brigade rules, would we find anywhere in the rules that a brigade has an area or a zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you cannot find it in that rule book. There is no reference to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sticking with this -- staying on this page, is there anything else that you find that might be useful for us to consider?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that almost every point illustrates the difficulties and the problems that were encountered in the process of commanding. The first one indicates that there are -- there is a shortage of officers at every level, which means that untrained, unqualified, unprofessional people occupied positions of responsibility. And that caused problems to all of us. And even the position that I occupied did not envisage somebody like me in that position. One usually starts in one's career from lower positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here, and just if we could go into private session for just a couple of questions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what else on this particular page that talks about the difficulties in the exercise of command and control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the next item it is emphasised that the area of responsibility is expanded beyond the brigade's objective abilities. So it is underlined that the brigade is not capable of defending a front line of that width and consequently cannot control what is going on ahead of them or behind. There were many ambushes at the time. There were many problems, all because our method of mounting a defence was bad because we didn't have enough people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Anything else before we go on to another segment in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also says here that we have no possibility for using any reserve for manoeuvring by the brigade commander. As I said, each of these items in itself is illustrative of the very specific problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me focus your attention later on further into this document towards the end. And for the ELMO, it would be on page 49, 00716479. Here it states that -- that would be page 17 in the English version. Now, it states here: "In relation to its establishment numbers, the brigade is at 128 per cent strength." How do you account for that? One, you're telling me that there's not enough personnel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has gone on for a while, but I don't see how this witness can really testify to these matters. I don't think -- largely, his answers are speculative. And, you know, I think it's gone on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think the first issue is that this question is relevant to our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. I think all these questions are relevant for a variety of reasons. We have Butler's report. If we want I can point out the sections in the Butler report where he talked about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I mean that specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, this question, Your Honour, with respect to 128 per cent, for instance the gentleman has talked about the lack of personnel. Now, one might look at this figure, such as Butler, or through his agent, you know, the Prosecutor, and say, well, see, at 128 per cent, how could this possibly be a brigade that lacked numbers. And this gentleman has direct knowledge. This is not speculation. He was there. He knows what was going on. If he's unable to answer this question, he can tell us. But I believe we will hear an answer that is very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It's my last question on this document, too, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to understand that sometimes something in the paper is one thing and something in practice is another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I totally agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you have already made your point here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I was just going to ask this one question on this one figure just so we can -- because I don't want anything being left unturned, any doubt in anybody's mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Okay. Turn that stone as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It says here "128 per cent." You are telling us that you lacked personnel, you didn't have enough for a second echelon. Can you give us an explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. First of all, one should bear in mind that this brigade was called the light infantry brigade. It's a huge difference between the infantry, motorised, armoured brigade. First of all, the difference is in the strength per establishment. I have no specific data, and it can be computed mathematically exactly the number of men that should be assigned to a brigade; probably be below 2.000 men. Now, in a situation that I explained earlier, that a brigade was expected to defend 43 [Realtime transcript read in error "4 to 3 kilometres"] kilometres long front, and as I said, according to the rules, a brigade in principle defends 10 to 15 kilometres of area. And that primarily refers to infantry brigades, motorised brigades, or mechanised brigade, or armoured brigades, so brigades of such type that have higher strength. This percentage of 128 per cent includes a number of men who were wounded or were in other areas for the whole time. For instance, we had people in different places that I wouldn't name now. This is just a simple figure which does not necessarily have to mean that at that point in time there were so many men on the front. And I'm sure there weren't. In some reports, it has been mentioned frequently where higher-ranking officers from the brigade command came to inspect the troops that the specific numbers on the ground did not correspond to those on paper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just one point of clarification. The record here says 4 to 3 kilometres long, but I believe, if I heard you right and if my Srpski is accurate, you said 43 kilometres long. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I don't have any further questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do have a couple other documents, Your Honour. It would probably be 10 minutes, tops 15. So if it's okay to take the break now and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could be in private session for the next two matters. If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to show you this one last document. It's -- we bring it out with most of the witnesses, D132. It's dated 4 July 1994. It's an information by Mr. -- by Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic. First of all, do you ever recall seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at paragraph 2 and sort of the last part of paragraph 2, there is a discussion here, information, as to attaining a final goal, an entirely Serbian Podrinje, "the enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde must be defeated militarily," and it goes on about the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave, making the enemy's life unbearable so that they leave. Sir, were any orders issued or was any policies in place that you were aware of while Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when Colonel Blagojevic took over the Bratunac Brigade, do you recall whether he pulled out this information by Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic and whether he had instructed the commanders and the soldiers of the Bratunac Brigade that this would be -- that he would be carrying out the already-existing policy that's reflected in this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We have this specific document of the 5th, issued by Commander Blagojevic, and everything is specified there. It is a purely military document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This one is predated by a year and one day, 4 July 1994. During that one-year period, were you aware of any activities that you were engaged or the others were engaged in pursuant to Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic's orders and carrying out this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of specific orders, and I don't know what that would mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you place any value on this particular document, D132, this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can just observe that it is an exaggeration. How can somebody link up different enclaves? Ognjenovic was, among other things, a journalist, so maybe he gave himself some license. Because journalists can blow things up occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've been told that. Lastly, do you have an opinion about your commander back in July 1995 and afterwards, that is, Colonel Blagojevic? Do you have an opinion what kind of a commander he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a very good opinion of him. He was an honourable man, an honourable officer. He was well-intentioned in his relations with subordinates, always ready to help. And certainly - I'm saying this in my own name - he certainly never ordered me to commit any folly in terms of what was going on in that territory. He was burdened with great problems at the time as to how to resolve the situation. He didn't have an easy time. I just want to point out on one occasion when I addressed him, asking him for help on a different matter unrelated to this, he told me: Mr. 2nd Lieutenant, invest all your intellectual and other abilities to solve your problem. That's all your commander can tell you. I understood then, and on many other occasions, that his hands were tied. A commander had huge responsibilities and very few abilities, very few means of dealing with them. The situation in the field developed often quite beyond our expectations and our abilities. We had a huge area to defend and very few people to defend it, and I wish to emphasise, an enormous number of problems. I also wish to underline my very positive opinion of Commander Blagojevic. Many other people like him would have been equally unable to deal with the multitude of enormous problems that he was facing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions. I have you very, very much for your frank answers. Mr. Stojanovic, who represents Mr. Jokic, may have some questions. The Prosecution may have some as well as the Judges. If you can be as frank and forthcoming with them as you have been with me, I would most it. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. And good afternoon, Witness. If I may ask Your Honour for this screen to be moved slightly so that I can see the witness while asking my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Allow me, only in view of your qualifications and your detailed testimony yesterday and today, to show you an excerpt from these rules of the battalion which you used in the examination by Mr. Karnavas. If you would please look at para 76 of the rules of the battalion. As a reminder, could you tell us what are the main responsibilities of battalion commander, the responsibilities that you had in 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are enumerated and specified here in a very concise manner. "The commander has the exclusive right to command a battalion and all the units attached to it for the performance of a certain task. He is responsible for the proper operation of the battalion and all the subordinate commanding officers; the status of political awareness and morale" - although we deleted political awareness later - "security, combat readiness; training; proper use of the units; and the execution of the given task."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point could we stop a bit. When it says "the commander of the battalion has the exclusive right of command," what does that imply?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That implies that no one but him is allowed to command in his presence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And a follow-up question now. Who gives orders to the battalion commander in terms of the chain of command and the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a brigade commander or his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be right in drawing this conclusion: That a chief of a certain service of the army would not be entitled to issue orders to a battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that should not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn our attention to Rule 77 on the same page. If the battalion commander is absent for whatever reason, the deputy battalion commander should stand in, according to establishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the deputy battalion commander is a person who has the same authorisations as the battalion commander in the latter's absence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he neither would be able to receive orders from the chief of another branch of service of the army; he would only be receiving orders from the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just ask you to turn to para 79, which stipulates the responsibility of the assistant commander for intelligence and security. Did you in your battalion have this position filled, according to establishment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What are the responsibility of assistant commander for intelligence and security on battalion level?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These responsibilities are enumerated in para 79.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For the record, could you tell us what those responsibilities are, slowly please, so that we don't have to tender this whole document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The assistant to the commander for intelligence and security carries out and organises the expert tasks related to intelligence and security support in the battalion. He monitors and assesses the situation, the intentions and abilities of the enemy, his intelligence, subversive and other efforts, and proposes measures to the commander to counteract such enemy activities." Shall I read on? I've read the most important part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The duty officer's responsibility was to convey your message to the brigade commander or the appropriate person. That was in the context of communications exchanged on the 11th of July, the movements and developments around your positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that it was the responsibility of the duty officer at the brigade command in terms of paragraph 66 of the instructions of -- on operations of commands and headquarters only to convey your informations -- information to the commander or the superior headquarters, only to forward what you have to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is not a person who is able to give you orders; he can only convey orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a situation, a last-resort situation, when neither the commander nor his deputy or any authorised person is available, and in that situation the duty operative officer can issue an order. But before that, he has to exhaust all the possibilities for contacting the appropriate superiors. And only after failing to find any one of them he can issue an order. But that is a very extreme situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if the brigade commander is around or the chief of staff is around or any one of the superior officers at the command, the duty officer is only to convey your message to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. For instance, the chief of the operations and training is number 3 in the brigade. So following that hierarchy, if none of the superiors is available, the duty operations officer is bound in such a situation to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in normal situations, the duty officer is only a relay transmitting your information to the brigade command and onwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may now draw your attention to para 147 of the rules of battalion. It is an area that governs engineer support within the framework of a battalion. Could you please, very briefly, give us an account, a description, of engineer support and who provides it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Engineer support provides some basic tasks which do not differ much even at higher levels of command, such as brigade. The first and principal task is the mounting of obstacles, securing movements by operating engineering machines, camouflage. These are the principle tasks, and of course security, fortification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. According to this para 147, it says that all this activity is to be carried out according to a plan provided by the superior command which specifies works to be performed by the battalion and which works are supposed to be implemented by the engineering unit of the superior command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would I be correct in deducing that battalions had their engineering support and in that sense they had certain tasks, as described here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. They had engineering support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This engineering support at battalion level, did it also include the possibility of mounting obstacles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, such as minefields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So battalion engineering would be the one who would put obstacles to secure foremost defence lines of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In ordinary units, in normal units, ordinary soldiers can do that. From the unit where I come from, every soldier is trained to plant an anti-personnel or an anti-tank mine. It all depends on the type of engineering unit which is built into a battalion or another establishment unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Speaking of engineering support, an engineering unit should be able to provide other activities, mounting obstacles, construction, fortification, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. This is all encompassed by the word "fortification."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would be correct to conclude that certain engineering works can be performed by specialised units within the framework of a battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DP-105 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. We have about 20 minutes left. Certainly that cross-examination could not be finished today, so I would like to ask the opinion from the Prosecutor whether you will want to start your cross-examination today and continue tomorrow, or we have an early break today and begin your cross-examination tomorrow morning at 9.00. Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no preference. I'm in Your Honour's hands. I can either start now or start tomorrow. I agree with Your Honour, I don't believe I will be finished today, so the witness will have to return tomorrow in any event. So perhaps it might be better to take the break now, since there isn't too much time left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's a good answer. Whenever I ask your opinion, you have to express some tendency so that will help me to make the decision. Well, Witness, I'm sorry that you have to stay here another day. I believe that you still remember what I told you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't forgotten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So the hearing for today is adjourned. And we'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.26 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 3rd day of June, 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
